description: Counting arguments, the pigeonhole principle and binomial identities

puzzles.title: \text{Prove the pigeonhole principle for } n + 1 \text{ objects in } n \text{ boxes}
puzzles.statement: \text{If } n + 1 \text{ objects are placed into } n \ge 1 \text{ boxes, some box contains at least two objects.}

blocks.latex: \text{Suppose, for contradiction, that every box contains at most one object.}
\text{Let } a_i \text{ be the number of objects in box } i \text{, so } a_i {{op:\leq}} 1 \text{ for each } i = 1, \ldots, n.
\text{Every object is in exactly one box, so the number of objects is } a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n.
\text{So the number of objects, } a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n \text{, is at most } 1 + 1 + \cdots + 1 = n.
\text{But there are } n + 1 \text{ objects, so } n + 1 {{op:\leq}} n.
\text{This is impossible, so the assumption is false.}
\text{Therefore some box contains at least two objects.}

puzzles.title: \text{Prove: a set with } n \text{ elements has } 2^n \text{ subsets}
puzzles.displayTitle: Prove: an n-element set has 2ⁿ subsets

blocks.latex: \text{Let } S = \{s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\} \text{ be a set with } n \text{ elements.}
\text{A subset } T \subseteq S \text{ is fixed by deciding, for each } s_i \text{, whether } s_i \in T \text{ or } s_i \notin T.
\text{Record the decisions as a binary string } b_1 b_2 \ldots b_n \text{, with } b_i = 1 \text{ exactly when } s_i {{setop:\in}} T.
\text{Different subsets give different strings, and every string comes from a subset, so this is a bijection.}
\text{So it is enough to count the strings: each of the } n \text{ positions has 2 independent choices.}
\text{By the product rule there are } 2 \cdot 2 \cdots 2 = 2^n \text{ binary strings of length } n.
\text{Therefore } |\mathcal{P}(S)| {{op:=}} 2^n.
\text{We count the } k \text{-element subsets of an } n \text{-element set } S \text{ in two ways.}
\text{Directly, there are } \binom{n}{k} \text{ such subsets.}
\text{Now fix one element } x \in S \text{. Every } k \text{-element subset either contains } x \text{ or does not.}
\text{Case 1, subsets containing } x \text{: choose the other } k - 1 \text{ elements from the } n - 1 \text{ elements of } S \setminus \{x\} \text{, in } \binom{n-1}{k-1} \text{ ways.}
\text{Case 2, subsets not containing } x \text{: choose all } k \text{ elements from } S \setminus \{x\} \text{, in } \binom{n-1}{k} \text{ ways.}
\text{The cases are disjoint and cover every subset, so by the sum rule there are } \binom{n-1}{k-1} + \binom{n-1}{k} \text{ subsets.}
\text{Both counts are of the same subsets, so } \binom{n}{k} {{op:=}} \binom{n-1}{k-1} + \binom{n-1}{k}.
